name: Beetle
lede: Beetle is a dark, greyed olive from a 1930 color dictionary, and the books have almost nothing to say about the name, but a great deal to say about beetles and color.

sections.title: An olive named for an insect
sections.body:
Beetle is a grayish olive, close to [[dark-olive]], [[bronze-lustre]] and [[olive-green]] on screen [1]. The earliest record in our sources is the Maerz and Paul color dictionary of 1930, plate 16 [1]. Why the authors chose the name is undocumented, and none of the books we read explains it [1].

The swatch here sits about 2.3 units from the ISCC-NBS block called grayish olive [1]. It is dark enough to hold a white caption at a contrast of about 7 to 1 [1]. The name may point at dark, bronzy shells in general, but the books do not say.

sections.title: The beetle that is not a beetle
sections.body:
Beetles turn up constantly in books on dyes, and the usual reason is red. Finlay writes of cochineal as beetle blood and describes ground beetles mixed with vinegar as a medicine for Philip II [2]. Gurney's pigment list says carmine is made from beetles [3]. St Clair counts up to 80 female kermes insects for a single gram of dye [4].

Strictly, this is loose usage. Greenfield places cochineal in the scale-insect family, and a wild one is about a third the size of a ladybug [5]. The older looseness was general: in the 1600s the word insect covered worms, slugs and frogs [6]. So the red dye that fills the books is a different animal from the one that gave this olive its name, and a different color.

sections.title: Color made by a shell
sections.body:
What beetles do make is structural color. Paterson notes that iridescence on beetles, butterflies and oil slicks comes from the structure of the surface and not from a dye [7]. Livingstone adds that beetle carapaces get some of their colors from thin transparent layers whose reflections interfere with one another [8]. Pigments absorb light; these shells instead shape it.

Paterson also records the tansy beetle, whose blue-green wing cases decorated Victorian dresses, and calls it almost extinct [9]. Nature charts used beetles as swatches too: a violet oil beetle shows Blackish Green and a small bloody-nosed beetle shows Pansy Purple in Baty's plates, after drawings from an 1891 British beetle survey [10].

To see it, look at a dark shell under a lamp and move your head: structural color shifts with the angle, which no flat swatch can do. Birren reports, after Vosburg, that yellow traps catch more Japanese beetles than any other color [11].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Beetle is one of the commonest dark neutrals in painting. It appears in 2,704 of 23,781 paintings, 11.37 per cent, and is more common than 94 per cent of our named colors [12]. It peaks in the 1700s, in 9.4 per cent of 3,449 paintings, 1.3 times the museums' baseline [12].

Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 46 per cent of 1,763 paintings, meaning a dark accent that sits between shadow and light [12]. Our most devoted painter is Willem Roelofs, in 7 of 12 works [12]. [[painter:edgar-degas|Degas]] and [[painter:jan-brueghel-the-elder|Jan Brueghel the Elder]] use it above their peers too [12].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and varnish pushes pale colors toward olive, so a match is not proof of a pigment. The earliest match, from 1190, is 740 years older than the name itself [12].
